name: PREMem

paper.title: Pre-Storage Reasoning for Episodic Memory: Shifting Inference Burden to Memory for Personalized Dialogue

construction.unit: memory fragment (key, value, date, message id) typed factual / experiential / subjective; plus reasoning fragments
construction.kept_as: LLM-extracted present-tense phrases; LLM-inferred cross-session insights
construction.processing: LLM extracts typed fragments per session with normalised dates; fragments are clustered per session and matched to earlier clusters; an LLM writes insights for each matched pair under five evolution patterns
construction.writer: same LLM family as the answer model, largest size (Qwen2.5-72B, Gemma3-27B or GPT-4.1)

organization.structure: two flat stores: fragments M and reasoning fragments R; session clusters exist only while building

management.operations: append new fragments; append reasoning fragments for each earlier cluster that matches a new cluster (cos > 0.6); a matched earlier cluster leaves the persistent pool
management.conflicts: not resolved in place; a 'transformation' insight can record a change, both old and new fragments stay

retrieval.query: question used as is (Stella s2p query prompt)
retrieval.selection: top 102 (token budget / 20), added in rank order until 2,048 tokens, then sorted by session date
retrieval.budget: 2,048 tokens in the main tables (1,024 and 4,096 also tested)

use.context: retrieved fragments as '[key, date]: value' lines, oldest first; no original messages
use.reasoning: single answer call with a short-phrase prompt

classify.note: Session clusters and the persistent pool only decide which fragment groups the LLM reasons over at write time; the read side is one flat dense search over fragments and derived insights. 'consolidate' because new cross-session insight items are written; nothing is edited or deleted.

stages.ingestion: Each session is processed after it ends; in LoCoMo each speaker's messages are sent to the extractor separately, in LongMemEval the whole session at once (code).
stages.construction: An LLM pulls out every personal statement as a fragment with a key, a present-tense value, the source message id and a date written as the message date, an absolute date, 'Before [date]' or 'After [date]', typed as factual, experiential or subjective.
stages.organization: Fragments go to a flat store M. For building only, each session's fragments are k-means clustered (k chosen by silhouette) and compared with a pool of earlier clusters.
stages.update: For every earlier cluster whose centroid similarity with a new cluster exceeds 0.6, the LLM reads both groups and writes short insights (extension, accumulation, specification, transformation, connection) into store R; matched earlier clusters leave the pool.
stages.retrieval: The question is embedded with Stella_en_400M_v5 and compared by cosine with every item in M and R; the top items are added until 2,048 tokens and then ordered by date.
stages.answer: One answer call reads the '[key, date]: value' lines and the question and returns a short phrase.

summary: Moves cross-session reasoning to write time: an LLM extracts typed, dated fragments per session and writes explicit insights (extension, accumulation, specification, transformation, connection) for clusters that match earlier ones, so a plain dense search over fragments and insights serves the answer model.
notes:
Venue: Findings of EMNLP 2025 (aclanthology 2025.findings-emnlp.1204, pp. 22096-22113); arXiv comment 'Accepted by EMNLP 2025 (Findings)'. Retrieval k and the chronological ordering follow the code (experiment_baseline.py L220-L231, model/utils.py L10-L55). trigger 'session-end': Algorithm 1 processes session by session; the released scripts run it in one batch over the whole history. control.management 'fixed-rule': the cosine threshold decides which cluster pairs are reasoned over; the reasoning itself is a prompted LLM (counted under construction).

headline: Memory is LLM-extracted fragments plus LLM-written cross-session insights; the answer model never sees the original messages.
The reasoning happens at write time, only for clusters of fragments whose centroids match an earlier session's cluster (similarity > 0.6).
Reading is a plain dense top-k over fragments and insights, filled to 2,048 tokens and sorted by date.

open_questions: On LongMemEval, removing Step 2 raises the score for three of six answer models (e.g. Qwen2.5-72B 67.5 → 69.8), so most of the LongMemEval gain comes from Step-1 extraction, not from pre-storage reasoning.
The paper does not say what the 'w/o Step 1' run stores instead of fragments.
Baselines are compared at the same nominal 2,048-token budget, but Table 6 reports 3.7-4.0k context tokens for HippoRAG-2 and 5.9-6.3k for A-Mem.

abstract.text: PREMem argues that long-term conversational memory should do its cross-session reasoning when memories are written, not when a question is answered. For each session an LLM extracts short, dated fragments sorted into factual, experiential and subjective information. Fragment clusters that resemble clusters from earlier sessions are handed to an LLM, which writes explicit insights about how the information evolved (extension, accumulation, specification, transformation, connection). At question time a plain dense search over fragments and insights fills a small context, and the authors report gains on LongMemEval and LoCoMo across model sizes, with small answer models approaching larger baselines.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

components.model: largest model of the answer family: Qwen2.5-72B, Gemma3-27B or GPT-4.1 (PREMem_S: 14B / 12B / nano)

ablation.src: paper Table 4 (LLM-judge; six answer models in the paper, two shown)

discussion.takeaway: Doing the cross-session synthesis when memory is written lets a plain dense retriever and a small answer model do well; in the paper's own runs PREMem leads on overall LLM-judge score on both benchmarks for every model family.

claims.claim: Shifting reasoning to storage time improves long-term dialogue QA across model sizes.
claims.evidence: GPT-4.1: 71.4 vs 55.9 (A-Mem) on LongMemEval, 67.7 vs 57.3 (HippoRAG-2) on LoCoMo. Table 2

claims.claim: Gains are largest on cross-session questions.
claims.evidence: LongMemEval multi-hop 83.5 vs 41.4 and knowledge update 93.7 vs 64.7 (A-Mem, GPT-4.1). Table 2, §4.2

claims.claim: Small answer models with PREMem match larger models with baselines.
claims.evidence: GPT-4.1-nano 58.7 / 58.8 vs the best GPT-4.1 baseline 55.9 (LongMemEval) and 57.3 (LoCoMo). Table 3

claims.claim: Extraction is essential and pre-storage reasoning helps.
claims.evidence: Without Step 1 scores drop 32.7-61.0%; without Step 2 LoCoMo drops 3.2-5.4%. Table 4, §4.4

claims.claim: PREMem holds up at small token budgets.
claims.evidence: At 1,024 tokens: 70.2 LongMemEval, 67.3 LoCoMo (GPT-4.1) vs 71.4 / 67.7 at 2,048. Table 5

claims.claim: BM25 and smaller construction models are workable substitutes.
claims.evidence: GPT-4.1: BM25 67.4 vs 71.4 (LongMemEval); PREMem_S 68.1. Fig. 2, Table 6

limits: Single-hop questions score lower than with direct retrieval of messages.
Original messages are not kept, so conversational style and wording are lost.
The contribution is empirical rather than theoretical.
reading: On LongMemEval, removing Step 2 raises the score for Qwen2.5-14B, Qwen2.5-72B and GPT-4.1-mini (Table 4); the consistent Step-2 gain is on LoCoMo (3-5 points).

The LoCoMo category names follow the code's id map (1 single-hop, 2 multi-hop, 3 temporal, 4 open-domain merged into single-hop; data/preprocess/locomo.py L178-L182). In the released outputs 'When did Caroline go to the LGBTQ support group?' is scored as multi-hop, so the LoCoMo per-category labels are not those most other papers use.

Totals include the adversarial questions scored by the LLM judge (LoCoMo 1,986 questions: the released GPT-4.1 run gives 67.73, matching Table 2), while the 'Adv Acc' column is a separate safe-refusal rate.
Baselines are said to run at the same 2,048-token budget, but Table 6 reports 3.7-4.0k context tokens for HippoRAG-2 and 5.9-6.3k for A-Mem.
The Full-history baseline uses about 18.7k tokens on LongMemEval-S (Table 6), far below the ~115k-token histories (§4.1), so it is a truncated history.
Every construction step (extraction, reasoning) uses the largest model of the answer model's family, while baselines such as A-Mem and HippoRAG-2 build memory with settings the paper does not state.
Table 3 lists Gemma3-27B Session at 33.3 on LoCoMo, where Tables 2 and 6 give 43.3.
